title: The Rains Break
body: After the long white weeks of waiting, the sky goes green-black at noon and the first fat drops raise the smell of wet dust that is the finest smell in India; and the whole district — man, beast, and magistrate — stands out in it with its face turned up. For one evening nobody is anybody's ruler. There is only the rain.

title: The Loo Blows
body: The loo comes off the plains like the breath of an open oven, and for a week the district shutters itself against a wind that can kill a man who walks in it at noon. You work in the dark behind wetted chik screens; the punkah never stops; and the nights are worse than the days.

title: The Cold Weather Opens
body: The heat breaks at last: the mornings come sharp and blue, the camp-fires smell of woodsmoke, and the whole exhausted country sits up and takes an interest in living again. It is the season of tents and touring and the year at its kindest. It will not last, and everyone knows it, and no one says so.

title: The English Mail
body: The dak brings the English mail — a month old, tied in string, smelling faintly of the sea — and for an hour the cutcherry empties as every sahib retreats with his letters to a world eleven thousand miles and one lifetime away. Then the hour ends; the letters go into the drawer; and the district asks again to be governed.

title: The Gods of the Copybook Headings
body: Ram Autar, filing the year's follies, observes that the same lessons come round with the seasons and are never learned: that the flood drowns the man who built on the sand-bar, that the borrowed rupee wants repaying, that the district remembers. He does not say it unkindly. He does not, you notice, say it hopefully either.

title: The Grand Trunk Road
body: Your tour crosses the great Road for a mile — the river of all India, running white from the passes to the sea, and on it every soul the country owns: the pilgrim and the banker, the bullock-train and the barefoot regiment, the holy man and the horse-thief, all moving, all talking, all magnificently indifferent to the sahib and his files. It is the most crowded loneliness in the world.
